title: Inputs That Fire in Step Are Kept

scenes.tts: A newborn ferret's eyes have not opened yet. Even so, its retina is already firing. Ganglion cells, the retina's output neurons, fire bursts lasting a few seconds. Each burst sweeps across the tissue like a wave. Then a minute or two of silence follows. Nothing is being seen. So why send this pattern to the brain?
scenes.visual: Ganglion cell grid in a retina; a yellow band sweeps across it, then silence on a timeline; a boxed question mark appears at the brain end of the optic nerve.
scenes.narration: A newborn ferret's eyes have not opened yet. Even so, its retina is already firing. Ganglion cells, the retina's output neurons, fire bursts lasting a few seconds. Each burst sweeps across the tissue like a wave. Then a minute or two of silence follows. Nothing is being seen. So why send this pattern to the brain?

scenes.tts: The wave moves at about one hundred micrometres per second. Two features of it matter for wiring. Cells near each other fire close together in time. Cells far apart do not. So when a cell fires reflects where it sits in the retina.
scenes.visual: A row of cells with a wave passing; a raster of spike ticks builds beneath, neighbours aligned, the far cell late.
scenes.caption: The wave moves at about 100 micrometres per second. Two features of it matter for wiring. Cells near each other fire close together in time. Cells far apart do not. So when a cell fires reflects where it sits in the retina.
scenes.narration: The wave moves at about 100 micrometres per second. Two features of it matter for wiring. Cells near each other fire close together in time. Cells far apart do not. So when a cell fires reflects where it sits in the retina.

scenes.tts: Now follow the signal to the brain. Axons from the retina reach the thalamus. Early in development, axons from the two eyes overlap there. One thalamic cell hears from neighbouring cells of one eye, and from the other eye. The two eyes make their waves independently. So the other eye's input fires on its own schedule.
scenes.visual: Three inputs converge on one thalamic cell; pulses from the two blue neighbours arrive together, the orange pulse arrives on its own schedule.
scenes.narration: Now follow the signal to the brain. Axons from the retina reach the thalamus. Early in development, axons from the two eyes overlap there. One thalamic cell hears from neighbouring cells of one eye, and from the other eye. The two eyes make their waves independently. So the other eye's input fires on its own schedule.

scenes.tts: In nineteen forty-nine, Donald Hebb proposed a rule for how connections change. When one cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, it becomes more effective at firing it. Now apply the rule here. The neighbours fire in the same wave. Together they drive the thalamic cell, so they are strengthened. The other eye's input rarely helps, so it is weakened.
scenes.visual: Two-cell Hebb diagram; then the three-input stage: the blue links thicken in green, the orange link thins and fades in red.

Now apply the rule here. The neighbours fire in the same wave. Together they drive the thalamic cell, so they are strengthened. The other eye's input rarely helps, so it is weakened.

Now apply the rule here. The neighbours fire in the same wave. Together they drive the thalamic cell, so they are strengthened. The other eye's input rarely helps, so it is weakened.

scenes.tts: Repeat this for every thalamic cell. The two eyes sort into separate territories. And neighbours within each eye end up next to each other. So the waves carry two kinds of information. Which eye an input comes from, and roughly where in that eye.
scenes.visual: Mixed blue and orange terminals in the thalamus sort into two bands; within each band they line up in retinal order; two labels name the two kinds of information.

scenes.tts: But is it the amount of activity, or its pattern? In one study, mice lacking the beta two subunit of the nicotinic receptor had no waves in the first week. Their ganglion cells still fired at high rates, but without correlation. The map in the midbrain stayed broad. Later work found altered waves in these mice under some conditions. So they lack normal waves. Keep the rule. Inputs that fire in step are kept, and the rest are weakened.
scenes.visual: Normal versus beta2 knockout: spike rasters (bursts vs dense random) above termination-zone curves (narrow vs broad); then the rule in two lines.
